Macroeconomic and political headwinds 
are whipping themselves into a storm: 
rising interest rates, a partial recession, 
bond markets defanging growth-oriented 
policies, and hefty inflation are being felt 
in every area of the economy. And the UK’s 
startups and scaleups are no exception—
as our latest data makes clear.
In some ways, this is to be expected. 
COVID-19 accelerated new investment 
(levered with cheap debt) into consumer-
focused, software-enabled growth plays. 
Recession threatens their user growth, 
and rising interest rates—causing some 
investors to exit the market—threaten 
their runway. 
But early-stage investing is meant to 
involve heavy losses, particularly in the 
Silicon Valley model. The UK’s failure rate 
has always been slightly lower, but losses 
are still part of the game. 
Some investment over the past 24 months 
has been frothy—it couldn’t last. But some 
of this asset class (more classic venture 
capital) is meant to be countercyclical. 
Investing in an early-stage, high-risk 
technology requires a time horizon that 
can defy macro uncertainties.
So venture investors need to be optimists: 
the current climate requires an adjustment 
of investment theses, but not permanent 
cessation. The success of the innovation 
economy cannot be measured in pounds 
alone: good ideas can win out, bad ideas 
will go bust.

Q3 2022 Equity Market Update // 01

The latest data on UK equity investment. We’ve analysed every 
publicly-announced equity deal over the past decade to spot 
emerging trends in the market in Q3 2022.
Investment activity declined, with £2.76b 
invested into private UK companies during the 
quarter, across 518 announced equity rounds.
Deal volume and amount raised decreased 
across every stage of evolution, alongside a 
significant drop in first-time fundraisings.
The cleantech sector secured half of 
megadeals announced, despite a 35% 
decline in cleantech investments overall 
All of the UK’s top high-growth tech sectors 
were affected: life sciences deal volume fell 
43%, while fintech funding dropped by a third.
Megadeals hit their lowest levels in two 
years, with just eight investments worth 
£50m+ secured.
Crowdfunding platforms fared better than 
other investor types, with deal volume 
dropping just 7% since Q2.
Around one in two deals continue to go 
to companies headquartered in London, 
accounting for 57% of all pounds deployed.

Q3 2022 Equity Market Update // 07

The distribution of announced equity 
rounds across the UK continues to be 
weighted towards the South. London-
based companies secured 52% of deals 
in Q3, while the South East received 
9%, the South West 7%, and the East of 
England 6%.  
Companies based in the North (Yorkshire 
and The Humber, the North East and 
the North West) collectively accounted 
for just 11% of deals. But Yorkshire and 
The Humber was also the only region to 
see an uptick in deal numbers from last 
quarter—albeit still shy of its record 33 
rounds in Q1 this year. 
Northern Irish companies once again 
announced the fewest number of deals, 
with less than 1%. Meanwhile, Scotland 
secured its smallest proportion of equity 
rounds since Q3 2016 (6%). 
London brought in a massive 57% of 
all pounds invested during the quarter, 
but it also saw one of the most dramatic 
declines in the amount raised. Having 
raked in £4.35b in Q2 2022, businesses 
headquartered in the Capital only 
secured £1.57b in Q3.

Investor types
Sectors
Every major fund type reduced investment 
activity in Q3 2022. Private equity and 
venture capital firms saw a 32% decline in 
deal volume versus Q2 2022, but were still 
the most active investor group in the UK’s 
high-growth ecosystem, with 234 rounds 
announced during the quarter. 
Meanwhile, the number of equity deals 
involving individual business angels 
and angel networks landed on 113 and 
38, respectively. Taken together, this 
too marks a 32% reduction in angel 
investments since Q2 2022. 
Having been overtaken by business 
angels in recent quarters, crowdfunding 
platforms regained their position as the 
second most active investor in the UK 
equity market. Crowdfunders announced 
128 deals in total, representing a 
comparatively small 7% decline since last 
quarter. 
At the other end of the scale, the number 
of rounds with participation from 
university and corporate funds fell 69% 
and 48%, respectively. 
The investment slump seems to have been 
indiscriminate across sectors: fintech 
deals declined 33% from Q2 2022, AI 
deals by 26%, and cleantech deals by 
35%. 
Having peaked in Q1 2021, spurred on by 
the COVID-19 pandemic, the life sciences 
sector saw a more dramatic drop in deal 
numbers, landing on just 20 announced 
fundraisings (-43%). While fintech 
fundraisings dropped to their lowest level 
since Q3 2019 this quarter, life science 
investments haven’t been this sparse 
since back in Q3 2016, when just 18 deals 
were announced. 
Emerging tech verticals such as edtech, 
consisting of relatively few companies 
and with few investments taking place, 
seem to have been less impacted by 
macroeconomic uncertainty. The edtech 
sector secured 11 deals in Q3 2022, versus 
12 last quarter (a decline of just 8%).
